q: Blue-grey compact marl in the western communes gives a Barolo that perfumes and softens earlier than one off the eastern ridge. Which soil formation supplies it?
exp: The Tortonian Sant'Agata Fossili marls under La Morra and Barolo hold water and give a rounder, more scented wine. The older Serravallian soils of Serralunga and Monforte carry more sand and sandstone and build a firmer, slower one.

q: Since 2010 a Barolo label may carry the name of a delimited vineyard site alongside the denomination. What is the official term for such a site?
exp: The MGA map put roughly 170 named sites on a legal footing, ending a century of informal cru names invented by producers. It records boundaries only and makes no claim about quality, unlike Burgundy's hierarchy.

q: Iron-firm tannin and glacially slow evolution mark the wines of one narrow eastern ridge in the Barolo zone. Which commune sits along it?
exp: The Serralunga ridge runs north to south on thin, pale, sandy limestone soils that keep vigour low. La Morra at the opposite edge of the zone gives the most fragrant and earliest-drinking style.

q: Counting from the first of November after harvest, a Barbaresco may not be sold until how much time has passed?
exp: Twenty-six months in total, of which nine must be in wood; the Riserva runs to fifty. Barolo's clock is longer at both tiers, which is the practical difference a guest is most likely to taste.

q: Of the thirty-eight months a Barolo must age before release, a fixed part has to pass in wood. How long in cask?
exp: The remaining time may be spent in bottle or in stainless steel, which is how an estate chasing a fresher style keeps oak influence down. Riserva raises the total to sixty-two months without raising the wood minimum.

q: Fruit from a young plot, or a cru declassified in a difficult year, is usually bottled under a broader Nebbiolo denomination created in 1994. Name it.
exp: Langhe is the catch-all denomination for the hills either side of the Tanaro and takes wines that fall outside the cru rules. Nebbiolo d'Alba is a separate and more tightly drawn DOC, and it excludes the Barolo and Barbaresco vineyards entirely.

q: Nearly all of the Barbaresco zone lies in three villages, with a fragment of Alba making up the rest. Name the three villages.
exp: Barbaresco itself sits lowest and warmest by the river, Neive to the east, Treiso highest and coolest to the south. The remainder is the San Rocco Seno d'Elvio quarter of Alba.

q: One Langhe vineyard was already being named on bottles in 1752, well over a century before anyone drew a cru map. Name that site.
exp: The hill sits in the middle of the Barolo commune where the Tortonian and Serravallian soils meet, which is the usual explanation for its balance of scent and structure. That 1752 bottle predates Barolo as a dry wine altogether.

q: Cinchona bark, rhubarb root and spices steeped in a Langhe red produce a digestivo often poured at the end of service. Name that drink.
exp: China is the Italian for cinchona, the quinine bark, which is where the bitterness and the name come from. It began as a nineteenth-century pharmacy tonic and is now the classic partner for dark chocolate.

q: Rose petal and a faintly bitter finish mark a red DOCG grown in a handful of communes around Castagnole Monferrato. Which grape gives it?
exp: Ruche is aromatic in a way almost no other Italian red is, closer to a Moscato lift than to Nebbiolo tar. It is grown nowhere else of consequence, so the wine and the place are effectively the same thing.

q: A pale Piedmontese red carries far more tannin than its colour suggests, because its berries hold an unusual number of pips. Which grape is it?
exp: The name traces to grignole, dialect for pips, and the berries can hold four or five where most grapes hold two. Skin contact therefore has to be brief, which is why the wine stays so light in colour while finishing firm.

q: Raspberry and rose scent a sweet, lightly sparkling red made around Acqui Terme. Which grape is pressed for it?
exp: Brachetto is an aromatic red in the Muscat mould and is fermented only partway, so alcohol stays low and grape perfume survives. It is the red counterpart to Moscato d'Asti in both style and purpose.

q: One grower in the Colli Tortonesi revived a nearly extinct white from the 1980s, and it now makes Piedmont's longest-lived dry white. Name the grape.
exp: It had been pulled out in favour of easier, higher-cropping varieties and survived in scraps of old vineyard. The wines start closed and waxy and take on a kerosene and honey character over five to ten years, which is why they are so often compared to Riesling.

q: Asti's bubbles come from a single fermentation of must in a sealed tank, halted while sugar still remains. What is that tank process called in Italy?
exp: Federico Martinotti patented the sealed-tank idea in Asti before Eugene Charmat built the machinery in France, which is why Italy uses the Italian name. Crucially there is no second fermentation here at all: the wine never finishes the first one.

q: Piedmont's traditional-method sparkling DOCG must be vintage-dated and rest at least thirty months on its lees. Name it.
exp: Pinot Nero and Chardonnay, alone or together, must supply at least ninety percent, with up to a tenth from other non-aromatic Piedmontese varieties. The vines sit high in the hills south of the Langhe where Nebbiolo would never ripen. The compulsory vintage date is the detail that separates it from most Italian metodo classico.

q: Dolcetto's most structured expression carries a DOCG named for a town in the southern Langhe. Name that town.
exp: Older vines on steeper, poorer slopes give a Dolcetto with real grip and a bitter-almond finish that repays a few years. Diano d'Alba and Ovada are the other zones where the grape is taken seriously rather than treated as an everyday red.
